strings.FWI_revfront_long: Parti Communiste Guadeloupéen - Parti Progressiste Martiniquais - Parti Socialiste
strings.FWI_Spirit_Third_Republic_desc:
Since the fall of mainland France to fascism in 1940, her colonial possessions overseas have met varying fates - in the case of the French West Indies (specifically Guadeloupe and Martinique), the Tréveneuc Law of 1872 was invoked, handing control of the islands over to several emergency councils that continue to govern them democratically and within the framework of the 3rd Republic. On paper, at least.

In reality, the matter of Antillean self-government is far more complex than it appears on the surface. The United States assumed control of the islands until further notice, using the Short-Fulbright Act of 1947 to provide a legal basis for doing so. While the Antilles may officially be self-governing, they are doing so under heavy American supervision.
strings.FWI_An_Ugly_American_desc:
They're everywhere nowadays. On your screens, in your newspapers, even in your damn government. You can't escape them. They barge in, no care whatsoever for what you may think or believe, and do what they feel is right.

Americans.

Lyman Lemnitzer is one such American. As the Civil High Commissioner for the U.S. Antilles, he has a pleasant face, a welcoming smile, and a can-do attitude; a veritable role model for policy in the former French colonies. But he is an American - a high-ranking one in the military, at that. And with that comes the issues endemic to American methods. His tendency to intervene in local issues has built up a rather tense relationship between the islands' existing institutions and the American Civil Administration. He is, in short, an intrusion. One that many in the Antilles find themselves growing sick of.
strings.FWI_Corporate_Cartels_Labor_Unions_desc:
It is no secret that the High Commissioner and his general staff all hold an affinity for the time of the New Deal, and this can be seen obviously in day-to-day life in the Antilles. Owing to years of New Deal workshopping, both capitalist cartels and labor unions are essentially political entities in and of themselves, especially when it comes to local politics.

In comparison to other United States-run entities, this is remarkable and creates a sense of harmony between the administration, business, and labor. However, this comes with its problems - should both elements clash or turn against the administration, it would be nigh-impossible to quell them.
strings.FWI_Stagnating_Plantation_Economy_desc:
In 1960, the United States attempted to recapture lightning in a bottle. American economic planners implemented an initiative in the Antilles called Operation Uplift, similar to the Operation Bootstrap initiative introduced in Puerto Rico years earlier. Aiming to invest state funding in infrastructure that would lead to a decidedly more corporate, commerce, and production-focused economy, administrators hoped that the project would bring the islands greater economic prosperity and increase productivity.

Unbeknownst to the high-minded pencil-pushers in Washington, however, this would only harm the Antillians. As workers left the plantations on the more agricultural islands in droves for the cities, there soon were simply not enough jobs left to go around. With a stratified class divide between the urbanites and farmers developing and the economy soon tumbling in turn, Uplift has only damaged the economy and led to a sense of lingering resentment amongst the locals.
strings.FWI_Squabbling_Few_desc:
Out of all the critics and rebels, Albrand's plantocracy seems to face only one persistent opponent, the planters themselves. Decentralization and favoritism made the plantocrats the nation's undisputed masters, and now there is no enemy to fight against but their own.

Coalitions, interest groups, and patronage networks spring up and spread out within the state's upper-class society. Though often only a product of tribalistic thinking, in search of sponsors, they often appeal to foreign powers that Albrand himself dare not meddle with. If this squabbling spirals out of control, Médard Albrand will enter the history books as nothing but a failure.
strings.FWI_Retreat_Planteurs_desc:
Plantocracy has been eradicated from the Antillean political sphere following Paul Valentino's ascendance to leadership, leading to mass outrage from the right-wing. Drawing from the Confederation's lower castes, the opposition now mobilizes against Valentino's New Deal-inspired platform by claiming the Prime Minister to be a pawn of American imperialism — a false populist stealing from the vulnerable.

For most Antilleans, there exists nothing as abhorrent as Jim Crow beyond the Mason-Dixon. The pro-Americanism of Valentino had made it easy to associate him with one of the deepest threats to the grassroots that the right opposition now appeals to. Whether it is slander or truth, this unintended baggage has soured many's perception of their new Prime Minister.
strings.FWI_Peoples_Triumph_desc:
Once created to preserve the dead flesh of archaic Europeanism, the American project of Antillean federalization has backfired, somehow being appropriated by Francophone socialists in the region as they take the lead in implementing the initiative, enthusiastically even.

Turning the tools of the oppressors against their own, the original institutions of colonial bureaucracy have been made a space of tolerance and good-natured fraternity by the various left-wing movements which it now encompasses. For the time being, West Indian socialists have much to rejoice over while their rightist kinsmen huddle in fear as red flags proudly fly over the Caribbean.
strings.FWI_Socialized_Colonial_Economy_desc:
The plantation economy was the legacy of colonialism and utmost humiliation. As a reminder of the Antilles' grimmest hours, being glad that it is but a relic is nothing short of an Antillean's civic duty. With the plantations' lands back to their tillers and its extractive exports nationalized for the masses' welfare, in a few generations, perhaps there will be no need for a state to hold its economy on cash crops alone.

As we now break our backs, the profits of our present toil shall sustain a million mouths in a better time. Nous avons osé être libres, osons l'être par nous-mêmes et pour nous-mêmes.
strings.FWI_Broad_Front_Opposition_desc:
The APF has truly become a symbol of unity, merely for an alliance not of their own. All capitalist forces now muster their arms, whether it be the cosmopolitan liberals, the unyielding planters, or the distinguished conservatives, none have any patience left for the impossible agenda of the Reds to make the Caribbeans their own.

Forming into a broad-sweeping rightist front with the sole goal of bringing one common enemy down, the APF faces severe challenges in all legislative actions as filibusters and boycotts grow increasingly frequent, and intolerable across all departments. Those who swore allegiance to the capital will not rest until they see to the socialists' removal from power.
strings.FWI_Beyond_The_Third_Republic_desc:
For all her nationalistic pride and newfound liberties, Antillean rule of law is but a morsel out of the carcass that is the French Third Republic, a name that evokes little but humiliation since its fall in 1940. The Black Power activists try and the nationalists nudge, but no movement can truly escape the legacy of the slaving system that their former overlord had ingrained through its existence.

None except the truly optimistic can foresee a future without French remnants, and neither do the socialists think it is practical to demolish all existing agencies at one instant. It is hard to tell whether it would take five years or five decades, but this time of decolonization is, regardless, the last chance to leave the old times where they belong.
strings.FWI_Exiled_Opposition_desc:
The cowardice of Parti Républicain seemed to have secured a brighter future in a blink. But in truth, it was never that simple. Those stooges for the slaving planters and their bosses, bereft of protection, fled the Antilles. They were not so much overthrown as they took the chance to migrate when the workers stormed their fields.

The PR and the planter elites might seem to be history, but they took with them a most potent weapon — capital. Fleeing across the Caribbean with a bulk of Guadeloupe and Martinique's wealth embezzled, they are now working tirelessly to call for their new government's destruction from across the sea.
strings.FWI_A_Revolution_Secured_desc:
With the failure of the counterrevolutionaries to secure their victory, the PPA can finally identify and successfully root out the remnant reactionary elements embedded within the administration. As the putschists' brief but tyrannical rule had pushed all but the most fanatical rightists into supporting Archimede's front, the revolutionaries are now finally in a truly secure position.

However, the dominance of the United States in the region remains a looming threat, and any missteps against its direction spell imminent doom for the revolution again. It is, therefore, an unfortunate decision that the Confederation must maintain a moderate foreign policy until there is a chance to get rid of the hegemon.
strings.FWI_Confederations_of_Federations_desc:
The Antillean nation is not merely a two-island confederation, it is an entangled union of two autonomous federal states with little in the way bureaucratic commonality. Essentially only in existence because of Guadeloupe and Martinique's unyielding elites, the Confederation's structure is, in effect, a mess of labyrinthine apparatuses separated in all their functions by a fundamental artificiality.

The product of this dysfunction culminates into an impossibly feeble executive branch in the union, one easily corruptible by local elites if they so choose. Can a government truly serve the people if it were no more than the same old gangsters in a fresh coat of paint?
strings.FWI_Outmoded_Plantocracy_desc:
Some people survive, yet never adapt. The plantocrats of the Confederation remain the single most influential group despite maintaining economic practices centuries behind the trend. For most of them, improving their underlings' livelihoods had never come across their minds, and wastes matter little so long as they can stuff themselves full.

These practices are despised by the majority of the populace, from the bottom to the top, who all perceive the plantocracy as being no different from colonial rule. But so long as the Parti Républicain cannot find a better backer for their ventures, this backward caste of lords will continue their rule over the Antillean economy.
strings.FWI_Victorious_Counter_Revolution_desc:
Supported by the planter aristocracy, the Parti Républicain has successfully executed its coup d'etat against the Archimède government to establish a new “liberal republic”. Returning in kind to the landowners' patronage, the current government has pledged to minimize its interference with the group's internal affairs as a policy aligned with its laissez-faire financial approach.

Despite nominal freedom of speech and commerce being upheld as of present, economic inequality grows rampant as government programmes shut down due to a lack of funding. An utopia for the plantocrats, but not much of a place to be for anyone else.
strings.FWI_Underground_Popular_Front_desc:
Following the illegal deposition of her left-wing cabinet, Gerty Archimède has gone underground with a few revolutionary militants in preparation for a full-scale retaliation against the putschists. As insurgents begin their offensive at the countryside, there is a fear amongst the plantocrats that the quelled opposition may yet consolidate into a true united front.

The Antilles is not a large state, and it will not take many to topple the regime as is, let alone being pitted against a well-trained paramilitary organization. Without further aid from Washington's hawkish sponsors, there is no hope for the Antillean government to survive this insurgency.
strings.FWI_Insular_Federalism_desc:
The unification of the Antillean islands into a single polity has resulted in an administrative strain that none of its individual constituents had the resources to moderate on their own. Under the advice of North American advisors, the Antilles opted to take on a governing model closely resembling that of the United States' federal-state system: individual islands treated as semi-autonomous states.

Characteristically, the executive branch of the central government is given significant power over the judiciary and the legislature, which are to be dictated by the islands independently, save in extraordinary circumstances.
strings.FWI_An_Ugly_Shadow_desc:
The White House can feign ignorance for as long as it likes, but after the dust settled, men merely turned into dollars, and the foreign occupation authority became the corrupt local government. Under the guise of humanitarian aid, the United States has all but vassalized the integral institutions of the Antillean government. Be that the military rallying around their America-trained officers, or the politicians seeking New York lobbyists to fund their ventures.

Colonialism is no longer fashionable, but entrepreneurship is. Northern businesses find in the Antilles a frontier to fulfill their vision of unfettered capitalism, and they will not let it go without a fight.
strings.FWI_Corporatized_Colonial_Economy_desc:
Progress does not necessarily mean improvement, sometimes it simply means matters have steered from its origin. The Confederation has made the reasonable decision of diversifying away from the feudalistic plantation system which the states had operated under, and in its place came a system of state-ownership, charters, and more assets on the paper trail — things of a corporatocratic imagination.

If nothing else, at the very least, a state-controlled system undoubtedly spreads financial corruption out from a few dozen barons to many hundreds of desk jockeys. It is assured to be good news that more citizens are getting a say in economic matters, for there is always a shortage of fresh minds in a modernizing landscape.
strings.FWI_Guilliods_Presidential_Republic_desc:
Democracy is a sham for the unwashed masses, a swarm of larvae and ants deserving of protection, but not the right to lead their own kind to a ruin which themselves surely shall bring about. In all their wisdom, the Guilliod cabinet has moved away from useless federalism, a system inherently hamstrung by the masses, to the more appropriate governance of a presidential republic, where the president is truly the first among equals.

Of course, the people should still have a say in electing someone they wish to keep in power, but it will matter little whether that name is Raymond Guilliod or not. All the strings come back to their puppetmaster, whether that be sooner or later.
strings.FWI_Strange_Bedfellows_desc:
A man of unclear inclinations does not gather many friends in a world of black-and-white, and enemies to Guilliod's reforms strike him from both sides. Red flags hate the man tearing their imagined utopia asunder, red necks hate the man for quieting a century-old economic lifeblood — meanwhile, the meekish conservatives are too cowardly to stand up for their friend in power.

Is Raymond Guilliod a centralist tyrant or is he a despotic strongman? That is a question to which none of the opposition can provide a uniform answer. But so long as they run the current course and crush whatever initiatives they see the cabinet pursuing, it is unlikely that the Confederation's status quo will stand.
strings.FWI_Antillean_Developmentalism_desc:
Guilliod's cabinet is not keen on giving in to the radicals or the reactionaries, no matter how loud they protest. It is beyond foolish to place Antillean livelihood beneath placating those few restless minorities. In the place of socialism and feudalism, the current pursuit of a liberal twin policy, that of tourism and privatization, has brought significant North American investment into the economy.

With foreign entrepreneurs being keen on turning a long-term profit, the Free Market gradually lards its own cogs into a self-sustaining model. The Confederation will prosper regardless of her naysayers!
strings.FWI_Actually_Existing_Gaullism_desc:
Raymond Guilliod is stuck in a purgatory of two mutually-exclusive friends, both of whom he must keep placated at all cost. The Free French exiles backing Guilliod naturally expected compensation from the cabinet, and in their process of finding high ranks in Guilliod's government to fill, they have built an atmosphere of cliques where each only desires to benefit their own protégé, with little regard for other contenders.

The other backer of Guilliod, the White House, is now displeased with the exiles for making inserting US-backed officials difficult, viewing their attempt of taking over the Antilles with little but contempt. Now Guilliod must act as a middleman between the Free French ambition and America's new colonialism, to drink both poisons rather than picking.
strings.FWI_forpol.1.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

OFFICE OF THE HIGH COMMISSIONER, US ANTILLES MEMORANDUM FOR THE UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE

SUB: UNREST IN FORMER FRENCH WEST INDIES

1. The political situation of the former French West Indies is steadily worsening. An economic program introduced by the Americans in 1960 under the umbrella of “Project: Uplift” to increase economic activity and help bring the islands into the modern market have instead had the opposite effect. The strength of the Antillean economy has declined in the last two years, with the project exacerbating a class-based divide between the locals. We advise Washington to prepare for immediate unrest.

2. This deteriorating situation has done little to endear the islanders to our presence in the islands. The insistence of General Lemnitzer, the High Civil Commissioner of the islands on intervening on local matters whenever he chooses has further complicated matters. The political gap on the ground between those opposed to American presence and those in favour of it is rapidly widening, as both sides have begun to resent each other over whether they choose to support the administration or not.

3. These tensions will likely worsen within the next two years. The Short-Fulbright Act of 1947 that granted administrative control of the islands will expire in 1964. Already, pro-independence and anti-independence advocacy groups have begun organising and campaigning, inciting riots, vandalism, and civil disobedience.

4. If the current relationship continues, then current tensions could escalate into something gravely serious. It is advised that the government maintains a close watch on the islands to ensure that the situation does not escalate further.
strings.FWI_forpol.1.a: Everywhere we go, there's something new.
strings.FWI_forpol.2.desc:
“Excuse me... excuse me, please, I need to get through... excuse me!” Jean murmured, pushing through the throng that had gathered in the streets of Basse-Terre. The moment it had been announced that the Americans were staying in the Antilles, there had been an eruption of anger across the islands, and wherever you went it was seemingly inescapable.

Jean? He just wanted to get to work.

Pushing up his glasses, he made sure not to make too much eye contact with the protestors. “Best to keep your head down,” his maman used to say, before patting him on the head and sending him to school. Coming from one of the more well-to-do local families but never amounting to anything beyond a managerial job at a moderately successful firm that came with the Uplift plans, he had never quite felt the need to partake in these displays. Either way, it felt as if the Americans would never leave.

Desperately trying to squeeze through a mass of sweaty bodies without attracting any attention, he quashed the irritation that was starting to brew. He could sympathise with them. Truly. Sure, this time they had promised that the President had appointed a special group of people to think about whether the people on their islands deserved independence or not, but he doubted many believed that anything would come of it. The Americans still planned on staying regardless - something their whole congress agreed on. It was an impossible situation, and Jean was sick and tired of it.

After what felt like an eternity he arrived at his workplace: a modest, yet official looking building. But as he approached, his heart sank as he noticed the sign in the door window.
strings.FWI_forpol.2.a: “”CLOSED DUE TO RIOTS. WILL REMAIN UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE.“
strings.FWI_forpol.3.desc:
General Lyman Lemnitzer was tired of losing control.

The General was used to being tested. It could be a soul-crushing job. He had bore witness to American forces crumbling in defence of the British isles alongside Eisenhower himself. He had been there arranging the terms of surrender, defeat weighing on his heart like a boulder. And when President Kefauver subtly kicked him to the curb by giving him stewardship of a pair of tiny islands in the West Indies, he had taken it with nothing but grace, endeavouring to manage them with dignity and honour.

And yet, as it turned out, he couldn't even stop that from going to shit.

He collapsed onto his hotel bed, nursing a glass of bourbon, neat. Going before Congress was nothing new to him, but it still always felt like he was a naughty schoolboy being judged by his teachers. As he went into detail of the situation in the Antilles, he could feel their stares and sneers. He was doing all he could.

Truth be told, the uproar on Martinique and Guadeloupe had dimmed somewhat, on the national scale. Once the initial outburst of riots and demonstrations after it was announced that the United States would maintain its presence on the island had passed, the tension had fizzled down to a local level. But now that independence had entered the public conversation, it could not be put away again. The jar was open, the cat was out the bag, and the pooch had been thoroughly screwed.

Massaging his forehead, he took another sip. It wasn't as if they had planned to occupy the islands forever, anyway. Soon, his duty would be done.
strings.FWI_forpol.3.a: Can't lose something you never really had.
strings.FWI_forpol.4.desc:
“This has to be a joke.” Richard Nixon's eyes kept going over the lines of the paper that he held in front of him. A proposed amendment to the Short-Fulbright Act, introducing a referendum for the autonomy of the islands formerly belonging to the French Antilles. A region he'd done his best to markedly ignore since the beginning of his term. “I'm going insane with this mess in South Africa, and you're wasting my time with... what? And you're telling me Congress passed it?”

'All they need is your signature,“ said the Vice President calmly as he pointedly gazed at the pen in Nixon's hand, which had been somewhat irritatingly tapping against the table for the past few minutes. ”The referendum is planned to be held next year.“, he continued. Nixon dropped the bill back on his desk, taking some time to massage his temple. He just wanted a break. ”And why exactly are we even considering this? We just gamble our hold in the Caribbean because of a few malcontents?“

John did his best to keep his cool. He knew the President was completely unaware of how bad the situation had recently been in Guadeloupe and Martinique. How it was a foreign policy crisis in the making. Instead, as usual, he maintained a trained, composed smile. ”Actually, the High Commissioner himself testified directly before Congress asking for some kind of concession to the locals...“

”Isn't that incompetent buffoon the reason we're in this mess in the first place?“ Letting out a resigned sigh, the President went to pick up his pen again, preparing to adorn the bill with his signature... but his hand stopped mid-track, as his eyes locked again on a small part of the text. The referendum's binding status agreement. An idea germinated in his mind. Some of the locals might not buy it, but a sham vote might help cool the tension for a little while, not forcing their hand to do anything about the result until they damn pleased. And if all else failed, he could always just send the marines.
strings.FWI_forpol.4.a: The next day, the unsigned bill was returned to Congress.
strings.FWI_forpol.5.desc:
The bar in Basse-Terre was unusually silent; a rare sight these days, even at this late hour, where the beachside drinking den was usually still animated by raucous discourse on independence and self-governance. No, tonight, the regular patrons had taken their protests to the front of the High Commissioner's residence, leaving the place solely occupied by its graying tenant Gaspard, with his old comrade René enjoying his usual nighttime rum in welcome serenity. A strong spirit that burned like hell and tasted even better.

'Short-Fulbright Amendment Vetoed', the headline said. In an even more unusual occurrence for a man who prided himself on purposefully ignoring the news, deftly avoiding political prattle, old René had taken to reading the day's newspaper to further spice up this peaceful respite. 'Following Presidential objections, the renewed bill passes Congress with supermajority, with an agreement set on a non-binding referendum.' René kept reading aloud, in a slightly amused tone. 'That's what the boys were arguing about earlier, right? Before they left.' he asked. 'Hmm-hmm' acquiesced the old bartender, without raising his face from the glass he'd been cleaning.

'I mean, I kind of get them. They must really take us for fools. Nothing ever changes, eh?' René threw a playful smile at his old fox of a companion, but wasn't offered any answer. Giving up, he turned his attention back to his glass, downing what remained in a single move, savoring every drop as his throat combusted from the fiery golden liquid. 'So... what happens if the Yankees refuse to leave?'

Without answering, Gaspard methodically removed the cloth from the now spotless glass to stuff it inside the half-full bottle of rum he'd been serving to his friend for the past hour. Then, he grabbed his lighter, and René's eyes widened for just a moment as the small flame danced ever closer to the liquor-ridden rag. Instead, he just lit himself a cigarette, not before addressing a brief wink to his dumbfounded peer.
strings.FWI_forpol.7.desc:
Private Cain was a simple man. A young lad from Ohio, with a fresh face and a sweet smile, raised on his father's stories of the horrors of Sea Lion. When asked what he'd do with his god-given life, of course he'd answer that he would serve his country and help ensure nothing of the sort ever happened again.

When he was finally enlisted in the US Marine Corps, he took to the vigorous training with the same determination that had driven him his entire life. He rose early, crawled in the mud and did what he was told, and none could deny that there was ever a more loyal recruit.

When they assigned him to the Expeditionary Force, his eyes were beaming with pride. That was it. He had reached his goal, and would dutifully help defend the ideals of freedom and democracy across the globe, freeing the nations of the world from the encroaching fascist threat.

When he learned that he was being sent to Martinique, he took it with the grace of a soldier. Though perhaps quite a far cry from what he'd imagined, he was never one for questioning orders. After all, the Antilles were still OFN territory, and he'd ward them with as much discipline as would be required to ensure it never fell into the Pakt's hands.

When he instead found himself facing a crowd of protesters was when he first started to harbor doubts. Even then, he stood among his peers with trained stoicism, and followed suit when he was asked to raise his M16, though perhaps at a more hesitant pace than the others.

If the swarm of indignant cries for an “End to the Unlawful Occupation” and “Death to the American Oppressors” were slowly eroding at his faith, he tried his best not to show it, just as he ignored the shake in his hands as he obediently pointed the weapon at the faces shouting at him.
strings.FWI_forpol.7.a: When he first pulled the trigger was when his whole world finally shattered.
strings.FWI_forpol.8.desc:
In the office on the top floor of the brand-new 'Royal Martinique' in Fort-de-France, a Westinghouse air conditioner hummed-an unaffordable luxury for the locals, but a mere trifle for Arthur Banks. The owner of a mid-sized hotel chain with assets stretching from bungalows in Bahamas to the perennially tourist-packed 'San Juan Plaza' in Puerto Rico, he was contentedly balancing his quarterly books.

The massive modernization program launched by Washington had turned Martinique into a gold mine for American capital. Banks had purchased the land for this resort for next to nothing, paying with generous USAID federal grants. For the first few months, while the hotel sat idle, staff salaries were covered by stabilization funds. And now, a laughable 1.5% tax on tourism revenue made his net profit nearly indecent.

Arthur flicked his cigar ash and walked to the panoramic window. Across the street, workers were boarding up the windows of a bar. But nature abhors a vacuum: a banner was already draped across the facade announcing the imminent opening of a Whataburger's. Vultures from across the States were flocking to the Antilles, and indigenous small businesses were dying out by the block, giving way to sterile, franchised eateries.

Independent economic newspapers were already writing: when the Washington tap runs dry, these 'investments' will never pay off, and the region will be engulfed in a devastating debt crisis. Banks, however, couldn't care less. Even if this bubble burst, his 'San Juan Plaza' was booked solid for a year.

“God bless America and Lyman Lemnitzer,” Arthur smirked, pouring a splash of local rum into his glass. Let the idealists and bankrupts weep for tomorrow.
strings.FWI_forpol.8.a: And Nassau is waiting for him.
strings.FWI_forpol.9.t: CBS Evening News Special Report: The Antilles
strings.FWI_forpol.9.desc:
“...And so the instructor said: the difference between an artilleryman and a diplomat is that the former hits the grid square first and apologizes for the miss later, while the latter manages to miss without even loading the gun,” General Lyman Lemnitzer's baritone filled the television studio, prompting a restrained smile from Walter Cronkite.

“Speaking of precise hits, General,” Cronkite leaned forward. “The recent triumph in Iceland. Washington is jubilant. But what is the true, global significance of this victory?”

“Strategic control over the North Atlantic is undeniable,” Lemnitzer stated flatly. “But more importantly, it is a signal to the world. The Organization of Free Nations is not the Reich's Pact or Tokyo's Co-Prosperity Sphere, built on the bones of slaves and the bayonets of executioners. The OFN is a family of free democracies. And we are proving that belonging to this family means being under ironclad protection.”

“A family of free democracies...” Cronkite nodded. “General, many critics abroad - and here at home - ask: how does this rhetoric square with your own administration in the Antilles? You've built a stable economy, but some call your regime in Martinique and Guadeloupe a mere military governorship.”

Lemnitzer's face remained inscrutable. “Walter, the status of these territories has been uncertain for decades. In a world where tyranny waits for our weakness, the United States must defend not only its shores, but the very foundation of democracy in the Caribbean. We have given the islands stability. And that is why, evaluating the work done, the President has made a final decision regarding the political future of the Antilles.”

A heavy silence hung in the studio - millions of Americans were glued to their screens, waiting for the verdict.“
strings.FWI_forpol.9.b: “Self-determination: We must respect the local choice.”
strings.FWI_forpol.10.desc:
The heat in Pointe-à-Pitre's Place de la Victoire was unbearable, but the crowd of thousands showed no sign of dispersing. Above a sea of straw hats, work shirts, and colorful scarves, the voice of Gerty Archimède thundered. The lifelong leader of the anti-American resistance was striking like lightning.

“They call themselves the shield of democracy!” Gerty's voice rose to a scream, immediately drowned out by the roar of the crowd. “But whom do they protect besides their own wallets?! Look to the North! Iceland - a nation the Yanks thought was their pocket base - found the pride to tell Washington to 'get out'! And the occupiers tucked their tails! If Iceland could force them to retreat, why do we continue to endure their boot on our necks?!”

Archimède struck the podium: “Enough! We will not let our islands be turned into a cheap casino! We will not be voiceless slaves like our brothers in Puerto Rico, breaking their backs for cents! Down with the exploiters! Down with the occupiers!”

The crowd of ordinary Guadaloupeans - dockers, fishermen, small traders - erupted in a thousand-voiced chant bordering on open riot. On the periphery, in the shade of sprawling palms, the objects of these curses watched the boiling sea of popular rage in silence. A platoon of American 'peacekeepers' in full gear leaned lazily against their jeeps, smoking. They didn't intervene. For now. But the Icelandic precedent had already done its work.
strings.FWI_forpol.10.a: The myth of the unshakability of the American order has cracked.
strings.FWI_forpol.11.desc:
The shuffling of papers and dragging of chairs belied the importance of this moment. Paul Valentino put down his files, straightened his suit, and looked at the first meeting of the transitional cabinet of the United States Antilles. These were the people who were going to guide the islands and their people to the future and oversee the final push from American control to an independent confederation. And he was chosen to stand at the forefront of that process.

It was true that the people of Guadeloupe and Martinique hadn't chosen him. Valentino had been appointed by the American Commissioner, Lemnitzer, and the American Civil Administration continued to function for the duration of the transition period. But this was still the result of a fair referendum among the people of the islands, and as the cabinet meeting began, with members presenting their points, offering suggestions, and even arguing, Valentino could not help but feel immense pride to be the first native the US Antilles to be chairing a government meeting. They were doing it, without the Americans-

A discussion on fishing rights between two of Guadeloupe's arrondissements was interrupted when the door to the cabinet room opened. Lyman Lemnitzer, the American Commissioner, stepped inside, accompanied by three more members of the American Civil Administration. The discussion froze instantly, and Valentino looked with trepidation at the uninvited guests. Surely, he thought, something was wrong. Perhaps there was a chaotic protest outside and the meeting needed to be adjourned. But Lemnitzer simply marched to the other side of the room, picked up an empty chair, and sat quietly. Valentino tried to return to the subject, but the ministers were looking to Lemnitzer, not him. The discussion could only continue when Lemnitzer, leaning back in his chair, smiled and said:
strings.FWI_forpol.11.a: “Please, continue where we've interrupted. Pretend I'm not here.”
strings.FWI_referendum_lost: The Referendum has ended and US influence within the Antilles is now unchallengeable once more.
strings.FWI_forpol.12.desc:
The assembly hall for the Antillean constituent assembly was lit up against the sunset, casting its glow over the crowd of distinguished dignitaries who had been invited to attend the independence ceremony of the Antillean Confederation. Outgoing head of the American Civil Administration, Lyman Lemnitzer, was the star of the show, glad-handing the Guadeloupean and Martinican notables and standing at the gates to welcome the American Secretary of State and discuss the development of the Antilles with him.

As the sun descended over the Caribbean, the doors to the assembly hall opened and the members of the new government of the Antillean Confederation stepped forth onto the porch, headed by incoming Prime Minister Paul Valentino. The attendees slowly quietened, before the newly-christened chief justice of the Confederation administered the oath of office.

After solemnly swearing before God and the attendees to faithfully execute the office of Prime Minister, and to preserve, protect and defend the constitution and laws of the Confederation, the chief justice placed the sash of the new office upon Valentino's shoulders. The usually stern man smiled widely as Lemnitzer walked up to shake his hand, as fireworks began going off in the night sky.

After the ceremony was over, and the chatter of men and women once more filled the air, Valentino made his way to the Secretary of State. “I wanted to thank you for coming here, sir. I am honored by your presence, as I have been for the help of the United States for securing our people's self-determination. I know how hard it is to be responsible for the foreign relations of a power such as the United States, and how thankless. But you have done the right thing here.”
strings.FWI_forpol.13.desc:
The people of the new Antillean Nation had spoken. Fort-de-France and Basse-Terre's streets were covered in blue banners and confetti, as its people celebrated the news that the center-right bloc behind Raymond Guilliod's PUG had won a majority.

Back at PUG headquarters, which was raucous with celebration, Guilliod was quietly enjoying his party's victory with a healthy helping of cane liquor. He felt a deep satisfaction knowing that Gerty's wacko communists and Valentino's lily-livered establishment politicians had been knocked down. Yet he knew that the threats to the Antillean Confederation's future was still not down for the count. Realizing their total defeat through the transformation of Antilles's administration would be the culmination of his government's agenda.

One of Guilliod's managed to squeeze past the other celebrating party members and handed over a folder. “Here's the report you'd requested, Mr. Prime Minister.” Guilliod silently opened it and began glazing over the report's contents. The papers inside summarized the PUG's plans to strengthen the Confederation through expanding the powers of the executive branch, the ultimate goal of which was the country's centralization and eventual transformation into a presidential republic. The strongmen in the region threatened his country, and the only way to save it was to become one himself.

Once again, the same assistant came hobbling over through the crowd. “Mr. Prime Minister, the American ambassador is on the phone! He wants to congratulate you on our victory”. Guilliod realized he'd been blankly staring at the last page of the report for almost a quarter of an hour now. He smirked, quickly shook his head left and right, and then proceeded to take a swig of cane liquor.
strings.FWI_forpol.14.desc:
“Another day, another victory,” Guilliod chuckled to himself. The front page of the newspaper in his hands read “NEW CONSTITUTION RATIFIED: GUILLIOD ELECTED PRESIDENT”. Many doubted this day would ever come, but then again, even fewer thought Guilliod's coalition would come to power in the first place.

The left would call him a dictator and the liberals would wring their hands over “creeping authoritarianism”; in the end, the Antillean people, the only group that mattered, voted in the PUG government's favor. The islands needed strong and decisive leadership if they were to beat back the sharks that surrounded them and pave the path towards a promising future, and that was precisely what Guilliod's reforms would achieve. By synthesizing the ideals of the 3rd Republic with an American-style executive branch, the Antillean Confederation's Presidential system would represent the best of both worlds.

One of the major aims of strengthening the executive through the new constitution was to overcome hurdles constructed by parliament, particularly as they related to new investment. Guilliod knew it was imperative that he facilitate the flow of capital and knowledge transfer to the islands if his country was to thrive, and he knew just how to get it. Guilliod ran his fingers across his rotary phone and called up his Finance Minister.

“Bonjour Monsieur le Président, comment ça va?”
strings.FWI_forpol.14.a: It was time to open up to the French exiles...
strings.FWI_forpol.15.desc:
As long as Jean remembered, there was always the big house. Its gabled roof sat snug on the white walls, elegant flower beds for feet. The windows were so fine too, but only the turning on and off of the lights could be noticed, lest he receive a blackjack in the back.

His dad remembered the same sight too, so did his dad, and his dad, and his own dad when he was brought off the boat and unshackled. All that's changed for Jean is the shackles were a bit longer, a bit looser, and the house got a new coat of white paint. In that respect, he was on the cutting edge of liberalization in the Antilles.

Of course, no one told him anything: he wasn't someone, he couldn't even vote — his ballot went straight to the big house. Yet, he heard whispers, what others told each other. He'd hear French voices spill hints, arguing about whose turn it was to run, mentioning the same few families running the islands. Recently, he heard American voices, ordering people around like products.

America, that nation that fought fascism abroad, that leader of the free. Jean didn't know what it was to be free, just that he wasn't, nor was anyone he was close to. Maybe, if they had a war here, America would come. And do what? He never thought that far ahead, not wanting to think about it, not wanting to think they would just put the blackjack to his back as well.

So, he looked at that big house — so big it could be seen from Washington — and got back to work for them. Maybe, it would be different for his son. Probably not.
strings.FWI_forpol.15.a: Big powers, big houses, and the little people in between.
strings.FWI_forpol.16.desc:
RESTRICTED/{date}

FROM THEODORE SHACKLEY
MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

1. Following the Parti Républicain's victory in the Antilles elections last year, our informants in Guadalupe and Martinique are reporting a shift in the party's activities. The PR attained the presidency through legal methods, and maintains the multi-party system that has shaped the Antillean Confederation since its independence. However, the party's agenda appears to be consolidating permanent executive and legislative authority through populist economic policies.

2. There is proof of large-scale corruption within the PR's government aimed at keeping the party in power over the long term. Planters receive sinecures and handouts in exchange for support, and across the islands the Parti is constructing local political machines so that the party becomes a solid, unified force for future elections.

3. Nevertheless, the Antilles' PR government strives to keep a friendly relationship with the US, leaving OFN-affiliated conglomerates and investments untouched at large and maintaining their security commitments in the Caribbean as a proof of goodwill toward Washington.

4. While the PR is currently challenging Guadalupe and Martinique's democratic pillars, the party is still far from being a threat to the region's stability or US interests.
strings.FWI_forpol.17.t: A New Day in the US Antilles
strings.FWI_forpol.17.desc:
The ocean breeze wafted through a nearby window as he listened to Valentino over the phone: “Thank you, Lyman.”

“You've noticed by now I'm not a difficult read, no?” former Commissioner Lemnizter said to his successor. “Congratulations are the least I can do, water under the bridge.”

Lemnizter could sense Paul Valentino's eyebrow raising on the other line: “Must be a large bridge, knowing where you live.”

“I wouldn't put it past the Yanquis to try building one.” Lemnizter rubbed his chin. “Always with the grand dreams.”

“I'd welcome it. Americans love a good work project.” Valentino ought to know; his help with the Confederation plan did miracles for Martinique and Guadeloupe.

Lemnizter blinked: “Socialist Party means to continue the partnership?”

“And with the referendum as well, they are not exclusive.” Valentino and SP were emerging as the preeminent party. Opposition across the islands was coalescing around them.

It seemed Washington's ally in the Antilles was set to become something more: “And the U.S. military presence?”
strings.FWI_forpol.17.a: “You've seen images of Colombia.” Valentino replied. “Whatever else they are, they are our protectors.”
strings.FWI_forpol.18.desc: Paul Valentino stared out at the sandy shores of Guadeloupe from the balcony of his vacation house. He had been working nonstop for the past several months, and it was time to sit back and enjoy the beauty of the island's beaches for a change. The sun was shining, the tide was calm, the birds were singing, and his administration's reforms were beginning to bear fruit. Empowered unions and stronger labor regulations would improve the health and sense of self-esteem of Antillean workers. Massive works programs employed the Antillean Confederation's people to build resort and leisure infrastructure that would bring foreign tourists out from their dull, grey countries and their money into the nation's pockets. Affordable housing schemes ensured that what were once slums would be transformed into real neighborhoods whose residents would be proud to live in. Yeah, things were good, and they were going to get even better. At the same time, Valentino understood better than anyone that these ambitious initiatives were being made by taking out equally massive loans from the Americans, and that this debt wouldn't be easy to pay. His Antilles had been under U.S. administration just a few years ago, and finding financing for the projects needed to develop the country wasn't exactly easy to come by. This all weighed heavily on him. Sure, the Antillean Confederation needed to be sovereign, but those responsible for the islands had to be pragmatic. That's what radicals like Archimède and Césaire could never understand. Bah, forget it, Valentino thought to himself. He knew he did what was right for his country. The prime minister puffed his cigar, took a sip of his drink, and sighed with deep satisfaction.
strings.FWI_forpol.18.a: Things are gonna work out just fine...
strings.FWI_forpol.19.desc:
The open streets of Fort-de-France were decked in red. Outside of polling stations, around bars and warehouses, and surrounding government buildings, the masses of the West Indies hoisted the fluttering crimson of peace, independence, and socialism.

Newly-elected Prime Minister Gerty Archimède addressed the people with a poppy red ribbon on her proud chest, voice floating above cheers, clattering pots and pans, and beeping cars.

“From this day and forevermore, we will heed not the slavemaster's whip nor the market's whim,” she said, and her beaming smile looked almost shocked at the great chorus of applause. “Starting today, the Antilles belong to her people!”

The islands would be in frenzied movement for the entire week, moved by the thousand steps of the popular front, from the communist party to the progressives, parading for the slogans of decolonization and development. The roaring, strained chants for equality shook the marble and wood foundations of the plantations, from which opposition leaders called for resistance and non-collaboration.

The U.S consul closed the blinds of his office, having had enough of watching the old street sign outside thrown out and replaced by “Anti-imperialism St.” The elections weren't even called yet, and still, here they were.

American expats watched from the concrete walls of the embassy, where they could still stand taller than the people. The masses saw and asked each other, slowly standing upright, “How much longer now?”
strings.FWI_forpol.19.a: For once they could answer, “Not long, comrade. Not long at all.”
strings.FWI_forpol.20.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

FROM FBI DIRECTOR J.EDGAR HOOVER
MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES

SUBJECT: RECENT UNREST IN THE ANTILLEAN CONFEDERATION

1. Despite ardent opposition, the pan-leftist government led by communist attorney Gerty Archimède has found early success in the implementation of its planned policies. Committed to a strong anti-colonialist platform, the rogue administration is vocally hostile to any perceived element of US influence, having severed all ties to the OFN that they consider as yet another extension of American imperialism.

2. While proving highly popular in the island of Martinique, Guadeloupe's larger population remains more skeptical in its support of the reforms. In particular, the dispropriated landowners of the former plantocracy have shown unsurprising hostility to the new regime, with some of its members covertly spending the remainder of their wealth to support sabotage efforts across the confederation.

3. The rising instability has led to an attempted putsch against the authorities in Guadeloupe, leading to the formation of a new temporary government by various opposition parties. The island remains the site of frequent clashes between socialist militias and mercenaries backed by the plantocracy. It is expected that an invasion force will be sent to Guadeloupe in the next few months to deal with the insurgency before it earns the chance to secure its position.

4. This situation leaves us with a unique opportunity. If we act quickly, a platoon of US forces could be sent to Martinique to displace the Archimède government under the guise of restoring order, ensuring that the confederation returns under our sphere.
strings.FWI_forpol.22.desc:
Through the car window, Lucette Michaux-Chevry silently observed the crowded streets that the vehicle was struggling to carve a path through. All around her, Pointe-à-Pitre's colorful alleys were filled to the brim with the cheers and chants of communist partisans and other sycophants of Archimède's clique.

Her bodyguards had assured her that the black-tinted glass was absolutely impossible to see through from the outside; yet she kept a lingering fear that even one of them could gaze right back at her at any instant. She couldn't shake off her mind the reports on the fate that occurred to other party members unfortunate enough to get caught during their flight.

Yet with the road packed with people and parades, they had barely moved at all for the past hour, leaving her with no other occupation than gazing at the city that feasted on her collapsing government. So she kept her eyes on the world outside, peeking at a cheerful group of teenagers who had gathered around a hastily graffitied, grotesque depiction of Uncle Sam on a nearby wall, his head popping off the hole of a mock guillotine.

All her life, all she had done, she had done for her home. For Guadeloupe and the Antilles. That had been the single constant that had driven her entire career, even until that ill-attempted putsch. She loathed the Americans just as much as any of them; yet she had been the one to swallow her pride and pragmatically try to tend to a lasting partnership with them. Ensuring their help and investments would help the confederation thrive. A dream that was collapsing before her very eyes.

As the jam finally began to clear, the vehicle started moving again. Yet she couldn't take her eyes off another graffiti on the side. Her own face, under which a single word was carved in bright crimson red. A word that kept reappearing in her head long after they left.
strings.FWI_forpol.21.desc:
At barely 30, Lucette Michaux-Chevry had clawed her way to the council of her small town of Saint-Claude, becoming the youngest woman ever elected to the position. The following decade, Guadeloupe's so-called Iron Lady had come to be known amidst the islands' emerging political scene for her raw charisma, ruthless negotiating skills, and her unflinching resolve in her fight for her home, until her meteoric rise led her to the close ranks of Albrand's PR.

When the confederation was finally ratified a year ago, it was a dream materialized: her long-held hope, to one day see the Antilles stand as an equal partner to the free nations of the West, just within grasp. Only for Archimède's goons to almost take all of that away.

In the street below, a grinning pair of US Marines was pushing a handcuffed man towards the back of a nearby jeep, where half a dozen more bruised guerrillas clad in scarlet scarves sat in silence. When the man refused to enter the vehicle, spitting at the face of one of his captors, she did her best to ignore the odd feeling in her gut as his insults turned to desperate pleas, squirming on the paved ground under the soldiers' blows. She averted her gaze, shaking away the growing guilt. She had done what was necessary.

Instead, she watched the last of the red banners adorning the streets slowly being brought down to be replaced once more by the waving star of the confederation's flag. And right next to it floated just as brightly the one of the OFN, with its promise of renewed economic investment and opportunities that would finally allow the confederation to thrive, while on the ground laid piles upon piles of the discarded crimson standard of those that had proudly taken a stance against that prosperous future.

Yes. Despite her lingering doubts, she found some measure of comfort knowing that in the end, it was still a victory for her people.
strings.FWI_forpol.21.a: ...So why didn't it feel that way?
strings.FWI_forpol.24.desc:
The building that once hosted the headquarters of the United States Antilles Civil Administration had been turned into a battleground; though perhaps of a slightly different kind than the one that had raged in the former French West Indies for the past three years. Instead of riot gear and Zhdanov cocktails, the battles here were waged with honeyed words, empty promises, fake grins, and firm handshakes.

Yet the stakes remained all the same.

The question of autonomy had gone from being debated in the streets to being confined to the walls of this improvised chamber, one floor below the High Commissioner's office, where delegates from the councils of Guadeloupe and Martinique were discussing the terms of their own upcoming independence.

The islands were to be granted self-rule, that had already been ratified; the matter that remained unsolved was the actual stretch of that very self-rule. And as always, none of the conversations happened outside of the ever-watchful eye of Uncle Sam.

It was an odd game. Whenever the councils negotiated among themselves, eager representatives from Washington would find a way to chime in on the conversation. Whenever asked for leeway in American control over the independence process, they would offer a sorry, but sympathetic smile as they reminded them of funny legal terms that made their request, understandably, far more complicated than it sounded.

At the end of the day, the delegates would come back home with their head filled with new juridical muddle that they'd never heard of, and without feeling any progress had been made toward their goal.
strings.FWI_forpol.24.b: The first step and certainly not the last.
strings.FWI_forpol.24.c: An ember of France relit so far from home.
strings.FWI_forpol.25.desc:
The last time General Lemnitzer had been in Washington, it was to sweet-talk half of Congress into agreeing to a scheme he himself half-believed in. Months of planning and preparation, of number-gathering, paper-inking, and repeating well-manicured words in front of his hotel room's mirror to ensure his arguments were as spotless as his smile. Today was different; all he had to do was listen.

His work had been finished as soon as he shook the President's hand in front of the cameras a few minutes ago. Now, he could just sit back and relax, sipping on a deftly grabbed glass of celebratory champagne as the President concluded the opening speech.
After a few further quips on the ushering of a new era in American-Antillean relationship were received in thunderous applause by the almost completely white audience, the microphone was left in the hands of newly appointed leaders Victor Sablé and Médard Albrand.

Not him, though, obviously. He hadn't been granted the honor to say a word for the entire ceremony. Not that he would have had anything to say. His years of efforts in the region had only been worth a few off-handed commendations earlier, of course omitting to mention the almost calamitous civil war that had narrowly been avoided. That was the extent of his importance, both here and there: being the awkward man in the middle.

He had just begun to notice how he had barely touched his glass for the past few minutes. Nor had he listened to much, honestly. More words on planned economic recovery programs for the now autonomous Antilles and US investment proposals just passed right by him in a blur as he kept on smiling. That was it. The epitome of his career had been to serve in a losing war on the hills of Britain, with the crowning finale of failing to hold the tiny pair of islands he was sent to oversee so they could get rid of him. He was nearing 68; he would never see another engagement. He would quietly retire by the end of the year, or they would force him to.
strings.FWI_forpol.25.a: And that's all he would ever be remembered for.
strings.FWI_forpol.26.desc:
The streets of Guadeloupe and Martinique had never, in their entire history, been as full of joy as they were on [?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong].

Fireworks had started being set off the moment the last of the American boats had set off in the early hours of the morning. For nearly half a week, the two islands were engulfed in a wave of celebrations; drinks were drank, parades were held, and tears were shed. For the first time in centuries, they had no foreign powers dictating their lives, neither French nor American. The two islands were finally free to choose their own destinies, independent from one another.

Of course, those native to the islands were not the only ones celebrating the newfound independence. As American boots finally drudged themselves away from the islands, sleek new shoes were quickly moving in to replace them. All across the world, people were noticing yet another potential chink in Uncle Sam's armor.

Local power networks would soon begin to shift. As the loud, bossy Americans began to leave, their vacuums would soon start to be filled by men from Madrid or Mexico City, offering friendship and solidarity. The situation on the islands had been blown right open - it was just a matter of who would step in to take advantage.
strings.FWI_forpol.27.desc:
Alphonse Dupré's fingers had long rubbed raw from handling sugarcane stalks. Sweet dust clung to his skin like it was seeping out from his blood. In the corner of the warehouse, a battered shortwave radio crackled with election results from Basse-Terre. Alphonse found himself listening to the tallies as he worked, hoping vainly for some sign of change. His spirits fell as the radio whined onward, minute after minute. Médard Albrand's coalition was sweeping the elections, a marker that things in Guadeloupe would remain stuck in the muck for at least three more years. The same names, the old Béké dynasties, rolled off the announcer's tongue, an echo from the poor youth of Alphonse's grandfather, and great grandfather. It was the obvious result. The one that all those who had let themselves be spurned by hope before expected. Still, Alphonse couldn't help but slump at his counter, his fingers falling away from the press.

Madeleine, one of Alphonse's few friends, perched on a crate of molasses, exhaled smoke into the heavy air. “So that's it. They'll never put down their whips. They'll work us and our children all to death. The Americans will booze themselves into the grave.” The grimy woman let out an angry laugh.

Beyond the warehouse walls, the harbor glimmered under muted lamps as freighters waited to haul their cargo north to hungry American mouths. Somewhere, an Iberian trade representative had begun drafting another contract. In Washington, a clerk ticked another box labelled “SUPPLY CHAIN STABLE.” The island of Guadeloupe settled into a familiar routine: harvest, transport, obey.

Listening to the new president drone on about a renewed parliament to lead the island into a new era, Madeleine roughly stubbed out her cigarette, and glanced into the darkness beyond the scratched window. “You ever think it'll change?” Outside, Alphonse could hear rows of sugarcane rustling in the warm night breeze.
strings.FWI_forpol.27.a: As the radio crackled off, the woman waited for a response that would never come.
strings.FWI_forpol.28.desc:
The streets of Basse-Terre buzzed under the heavy Caribbean sun as radios roared out with the unbelievable. Against all forecasts, the entrenched Albrand coalition had fallen in the most recent election. In its place, the fiery populist leader Raymond Guilliod surged into first place, triumphing in the polls with his tantalizing offer of change to a desperate population. His program, which he delivered in a series of fervent addresses across the island, promised national reform and an end to corruption, state-building, and the reduction of foreign control. In the streets, the crowds gathered in the capital's central marketplace were beginning impromptu celebrations, with supporters quickly overwhelming the limited police force.

In his packed campaign office, Raymond Guilliod leaned over his desk, blissfully unaware of the pandemonium his victory was provoking outside. Sweat dripped onto maps of the island's neglected roads and ports. Steeling his resolve, the man moved to the dingy microphone in the room and signalled to an aide to begin his broadcast. It was time to address the hungry nation.

“People of Guadeloupe, we have heard your voice!” Raymond thundered into the radio, speaking to it as though it was a roaring crowd of hundreds. “I promise you this: this election is no empty promise! No more of the same. It is time for the people of this island to own the land we work on. It is time to build our nation, not strip it for parts to sell overseas. My people, now is the time for hope. Our journey has only just begun.” Around him, his aides exchanged nervous glances, fearful that success had not seemed to curb the man's radicalism. Despite the coming American backlash, though, a sense of hope had filled the room.

Outside, an uproar emerged among the crowds of the capital in response to the broadcast. People began chanting Guilliod's name, pushing against the stalls of the market in a frenzy.

Across the sea, the atmosphere was somber. Iberian and Mexican diplomats wrote tense telegrams discussing the development. In Washington, a clerk underlined a single phrase in red ink: “potentially hostile executive.” The island had begun to shift.
strings.FWI_forpol.29.desc:
The grandeur of the Organization of Free Nation's central assembly hall in New York was pierced only by the echoing of footsteps as President Albrand and his delegation approached the elaborate dais under the gaze of hundreds of eyes. The Guadeloupean flag, hastily stitched and still stiff, hung beside the stars-and-stripes and the shimmering blue OFN banner that dominated the wall and ceiling in the back of the hall.

An OFN commissioner stepped forward, offering a handshake to the President. “On this day, the Organization of Free Nations formally welcomes Guadeloupe into its alliance. May our partnership help safeguard freedom and prosperity in the world.”

Finally dropping the handshake, the gray-haired former president stepped forward and addressed the assembly. “Honorable representatives of the OFN, Guadeloupe extends a warm thanks to all who have offered aid to our new nation and sent congratulations following our recent election. We look forward to strengthening our ties with all free nations of the world. Despite our small size, it is my firm hope that you will all soon see Guadeloupe as your equals in the fight for freedom.”

At the back, a junior delegate from the United States murmured to the man next to him. “Equals?”

A thin smile answered. “Equal enough that they'll keep the ships humming along. That's what matters.”

The signatures were penned, the cameras flashed, and reserved applause rose from most in the hall. Beyond the high windows, a light rain traced silver streaks against the skyline. The Caribbean's newest OFN partner had just accepted its place in the bulwark.
strings.FWI_forpol.29.a: Wars are won by small victories.
strings.FWI_forpol.30.desc:
“So... are we really doing this?” There was an uncomfortable tension in the corridor. Politely waiting in front of the desk upon which stood the deal, the representative from the United Mexican States anxiously shifted from one side of the chair to the other as the two of them had stepped outside to ponder a little more.

“Again: a temporary partnership. Nothing more. One born out of shared interests and common foes.”, she dismissed with a hand wave. In truth, Gerty Archimède felt just as unsure as her foreign minister. Yes, it was an odd choice of partner, and most definitely a far cry from their own platform of revolutionary anti-colonialism; but the Mexicans remained aligned with their aims of eroding the American sphere. Still, neither of them could shake away the feeling that they were just about to replace one master with another.

“The boys aren't going to buy that, and you know it very well”, he concluded, before entering the room again. “I... just hope you're making the right choice.” Despite barely months ago, it felt like an eternity since they had torn the broken left away from Valentino's sinking ship. Allying themselves with the reformist cowards of the PS had already felt like a small betrayal; and she, too, feared that they were already brewing a second one.

Yet, however loudly they had cheered after the coalition led by their own party had won last year's election, and however high the poppy banners now floated along the streets of Basse-Terre in scarlet defiance against American hegemony; the truth was, Guadeloupe was small. And alone. They needed allies; and anything was better than the Yankees, right?

“I hope so too,” were the words she wished she could have answered before the pen had finished inking the paper, prompting an eager smile from the Mexican envoy who stood up to shake their hands.
strings.FWI_forpol.30.a: Welcome to the Pact of Veracruz.
strings.FWI_forpol.31.desc:
Mirroring the streets of Fort-De-France, across which newly erected red banners flowed over the singing crowds, the headquarters of the Parti Progressiste Martiniquais were abuzz with raucous cheers and chants after the election results had slowly unraveled.

On Aimé Césaire's desk, a newspaper whose headline confirmed the sweeping victory achieved by the socialist coalition. And not only had it propelled itself at the head of the newly sovereign island, but it had done so in a way that entrenched it with a certain majority in Martinique's legislative council, smothering any hope for Sablé's liberal bloc and other US-backed opposition groups to block their incoming radical reforms.

Yet, a noticeable absent from the ongoing festivities was the man himself. Despite the best efforts of his party's co-members, he remained stuck in his room, lost in thought, reluctant to partake in the celebrations or even share their enthusiasm about their landslide success. In fact, he struggled to consider it a victory at all.

Victory would come when the people of Martinique would be finally freed from any trace of the American grip, followed by the rest of their comrades scattered across the Antilles and the West Indies. It went even further than that; victory would come when black consciousness had finally taken root in all the African diaspora. And not just them; when each and every individual now suffering under colonial yoke all across the world would be freed from their chains. When the future that had been stolen from them would be taken back by grasping at their masters' throats.

No, it was no victory at all; not yet, at any rate. For their tiny home of Martinique to become this shining red beacon against imperialism, they would have to wait longer still. Play nice with the Yankees. Share their pretty smiles and shake their hands while hiding the daggers behind their back. So for now, all he could do was bide his time...
strings.FWI_forpol.31.a: ...and hope it was only the calm before the coming storm.
strings.FWI_forpol.32.desc:
Across Martinique, thousands were huddled around radios and the occasional television. Through commentator description or live feed, all were fixed upon the same spot, all at the gates of Martinique Prefecture Hotel. It was thronged with jostling journalists and waiting watchers, all trying to get a preferential view of the speaker's microphone. None watched more intently than those at the embassies, every official watching or listening above piles of assessments attempting to predict the future.

Victor Sablé. Who was he? What was he? Who were his friends?

Radio journalists spoke quickly into their microphones as Sablé approached the gates that swung open to meet him, a cheer from some of those watching beckoning him to the set up microphones. His mirth was evident; he grinned into the TV cameras and smiled at the audience. “Ladies and Gentleman,” he began, “I come to tell you today about our future.”

“I want to thank every person who placed their faith in the Parti Républicain. I swear to you all that Martinique shall not become a small nation dominated by despots obeying foreign whims. My vision, to share with you all, is a Martinique where all are truly free. Where the government and the economy work hand in hand and our affairs are discussed openly through the assembly, not in some shady backroom. Where all classes come together, realizing that regardless of condition or status; we are all of Martinique.” He paused, cameras flashing around him.

“To my friends that support me in this mission, to our OFN friends that helped us to come this far, I say thank you. To those who wish to bend me against the interests of my national family, I say I shall stand against you. To those who have placed their well-being, the well-being of their family and the well-being of their future in me, I say that I will give all that I can for you.”
strings.FWI_forpol.32.a: Quotations colored reports from Washington to Madrid, with very different descriptions
strings.FWI_forpol.33.desc:
From beneath a broad tent erected in La Savane park, Tertulien Robinel, head of the Socialist Federation of Martinique, addressed a sea of umbrellas in the pattering rain. “The Civil Administration has passed. And I am proud that you, the people of Martinique, have chosen myself and the FSM, to lead you through these first, critical years of independence. Today, you have chosen a new future for Martinique - one of rapid and thorough reform. Social, economic, political. One where the people own the farms and the factories where they labor, and where the fruits of that labor belongs to them.”

Out of the corner of his eye, he could see the U.S. ambassador squirming in the front row of folding chairs, flanked by his rather-more pleased Mexican counterpart and a stone-faced Iberian.

But this speech was not for them. He looked out at the crowd, at all the exuberant faces of Fort-de-France. From humble workers, who had trusted his steady promises over the wild revolution offered by the PPM, to sharply-dressed bureaucrats and professionals, who defected from the hithero dominant Parti Républicain, Robinel sought the words to unite them all.

“To Martinique! May her prosperity grow as green and as open as La Savane!
strings.FWI_forpol.33.a: In Martinique, the middle-of-the-road is on the left.
strings.FWI_forpol.34.desc:
Tertulien Robinel strode through the doors of the OFN headquarters, shrugging off his heavy coat to the waiting doorman with a smile. New York... New York was cold. Cold for a man from Martinique. Wall Street colder still to a socialist who had nationalized vast swathes of an island economy, and taxed what remained in private hands to fund his development program.

In here though... everything was warm. Each hand proffered to him, most pudgy and white, heated his frigid black fingers. Smiles and nods from the host of diplomats congratulating Robinel on his second term, on the solidification of Martinique's democracy.

He imagined that the toasts, the toasts welcoming his island nation would be with champagne. But after all the years spent waiting, calling, writing, and cajoling to show that Martinique was indeed worthy of being part of the Organization of Free Nations, Robinel felt comfortable, entitled even, to approach a suited member of the building's staff, put on an easy smile, and say,

“One mulled wine, please.”
strings.FWI_forpol.35.desc:
Excerpt from a recent translation exercise from a university level French course:

'A peculiar coalition of Francophiles, liberals, reactionaries, and landowners has taken power in Martinique under the UPM led by Edmond Valcin. The new government has begun to attempt to restructure their movement into a proper party, though they have replaced many public servants in their attempts to do so, further destabilizing their rule. Backed by Iberia, the new Martinique is by far the strangest of the bloc's allies, the island nation being nominally progressive and democratic. So far though, they have managed to resist collapse and are embracing themselves as a unique gem in the crown of the Caribbean. What is left of Free France has taken an immense interest in the island nation and the two have reportedly been having talks for quite some time. What the future of Martinique looks like is anyone's guess, but it certainly worth keeping an eye on.'

'France is alive, somewhere at least.'
strings.FWI_forpol.35.a: Where is our professor getting news from Martinique?
strings.FWI_forpol.36.desc:
Guilliod stood at the open shutters of the old governor's hall, staring at the harbor below. The sunset washed the water in gold, casting the freighters, heavy with sugar and rum bound for America, in brilliant light. His brain was buzzing from the speech he had just delivered, demanding sovereignty for the nation of Guadeloupe and formally dissolving the defensive pacts binding the island to the United States. With the people's support confirmed in last year's election and his growing power in the executive, he was more certain than ever that it was time to chart a new course for the nation.

A knock at the door. His foreign minister slipped inside, face drawn tight. “The Americans are furious. The Iberians...” He hesitated. “They're interested. One of their envoys has arrived downstairs. The French have also sent a telegram. It seems your declaration has caught their attention.”

Guilliod turned back to the window, letting the humid air press against the satisfaction etched on his face. “Let them sweat for a moment. It's good to let our former masters pace.” He poured himself a measure of cane liquor and downed it in a single swallow. After a few minutes, he finally turned back and opened the door to the lower floor. It was time to reap the benefits of Guadeloupe's independence.
strings.FWI_news.1.desc:
Martinique and Guadeloupe are rocked by red parades today, as newly-elected Prime Minister Gerty Archimède announced the Antillean Confederation's independence. This marks the end of years of U.S occupation, and centuries of colonialism, and the beginning of a new page in the difficult history of the West Indies.

Washington has issued a muted response, expressing concern for the safety of American citizens and Archimède's political opponents in the islands. Tense popular demonstrations have surrounded the U.S embassy, but as international congratulations flow in, the people seem more concerned with cheering the new government's slogan of development, decolonization, and equality.
strings.FWI_news.1.d: A small blow to U.S hegemony...
strings.FWI_news.2.desc:
Martinique and Guadeloupe are rocked by parades today, as newly re-elected Prime Minister Paul Valentino announced the Antillean Confederation's independence. This marks the end of years of U.S. governance over the Islands, and the beginning of a new page in the difficult history of the West Indies. Valentino's government was quick to reaffirm the Confederation's special relationship with the United States, as the newly independent islands continue to rely heavily on the Americans for defense.

Washington welcomed the announcement, as while they may no longer run the Antilles directly, the U.S. can rest assured knowing its influence over Caribbean affairs will remain largely intact, now without the burdens of responsibility over the islands' administration.
strings.FWI_news.2.c: Independence at last, but is it just an illusion?
strings.FWI_news.3.t: {get_newspaper_header}Antillean Confederation Gains Independence from the United States
strings.FWI_news.3.desc:
President Paul Valentino of the Antillean Confederation has announced in an address that the islands, long under the rule of the United States, have “joined the free nations of the world.” Head of the Parti Républicain (PR), Paul Valentino has led the party to stunning victory in the islands of Martinique and Guadeloupe.

While still firmly tied to the US, the Antillean Confederation has now reaped the benefits from its new integration into the world market, a long held promise by the PR. Along with free trade, the PR has promised to build up the institutions of the islands, while creating an inter-class political base for the party.

With the immense success in the recent elections, the PR may be in charge of the Antilles Confederation for years to come, with some leftist critics calling the nation a one party state.
strings.FWI_news.4.t: {get_newspaper_header}Antillean Confederation Declares Independence from United States
strings.FWI_news.4.desc:
This morning, hundreds of thousands of Antilleans woke up to their new president, Raymond Guilliod of the Parti Unifié Guadeloupéen (PUG) party. As a new dawn shines over the now independent Antillean Confederation, Guilliod seeks to move away from American influence.

During his campaign, Guilliod has emphasized heavy-handed policies to promote a new French Antillean identity along with grassroots national development outside of America's sphere. Notably, Guilliod has pushed for Creole education within its schools and encouraged tourism of Creole and French heritage sites.

The world—especially America—looks at the new nation with anticipation. Although another batch of maps has been made obsolete, a new one is being etched within the hearts and souls of Antilleans.
strings.FWI_news.4.a: We will respect their choice as long as they respect us.
strings.FWI_news.5.desc:
