Shock waves reverberated in the waters of the Caribbean today as the small island nation of Guadeloupe officially declared independence from its protector, the United States, loosening long-term economic and political ties. Prime Minister Médard Albrand, who has long dominated the island's politics, pledged to carry forward the democratic traditions of the exiled French Republic as Guadeloupe enters the world stage as a sovereign nation.

Despite the surprise of the announcement, analysts report that the ruling coalition is still firmly in control of the political apparatus in the country, and that sugar and rum exports to the United States are not likely to decrease. For many on the island, doubt remains on whether this declaration will bring about any lasting changes.
strings.FWI_news.6.t: {get_newspaper_header}Guadeloupe Severs Ties with the United States
strings.FWI_news.6.desc:
Shock travelled north across the Caribbean today as the island of Guadeloupe officially declared independence, severing decades-long ties between the United States and the island's French plantation owners. The announcement came under the auspices of the newly victorious Parti d'Unité Gaulliste (PUG), a populist conservative movement led by the fiery Raymond Guilliod.

In his address, Guilliod pledged to expand domestic ownership of industry, build a strong state apparatus, and pursue an independent foreign policy. Analysts in the region note that Guilliod's multi-ethnic backing reflects the island's growing shift towards self-determination and racial liberation, trends mirrored closely across the Caribbean. Though Washington expressed “measured concern,” Guilliod's speech offered continued trade with the United States if “significant rebalancing” was involved. The president concluded his address by declaring a new era for Guadeloupean sovereignty.
strings.FWI_news.6.a: We wish them luck — they'll need it!
strings.FWI_news.7.desc:
In the aftermath of the historic referendum taken in the former US Administration of the Antilles, and the subsequent dissolution of the Civil Administration, the island-nation of Martinique has inaugurated its independence with its first ever election. Now under the bold rule of the charismatic socialist Aimé Césaire, the island has both nominally and practically separated from the United States and former master France, and faces an uncertain future isolated in the region.

International observers, initially predicting a win for opposition leader Victor Sablé and a smooth reintegration into the OFN, now note Césaire's strong socialist stance and opposition to most American prerequisites to aid. Attempts to draft a treaty of friendship with the US have failed in the Conseil Général, and it is unlikely that the experiment will be revived. Martinique will march a lonely road ahead, separated from the rest of its peers in the Caribbean protected under the long shadow of Washington.
“
strings.FWI_news.7.a: Bold move for a little island.
strings.FWI_news.9.desc:
In the aftermath of the historic referendum taken in the former US Administration of the Antilles, and the subsequent dissolution of the Civil Administration, the island-nation of Martinique has inaugurated its independence with its first ever election. Now under the control of the liberal candidate Victor Sablé, the island has nominally separated from both the United States and France, though retaining extremely strong American ties.

International observers had predicted Sablé's victory even before polls began, noting his platform of liberal developmentalism built on much the same grounds as the American Democratic party. The island has acceded to the OFN, and will likely soon host a small military delegation. Though some decry foreign influence, Sablé's programme of national development funded through foreign aid and development of institutions remains popular and grants his party a blank cheque to lead the country through its tenuous first years of independence.
strings.FWI_news.10.desc:
In the aftermath of the historic referendum taken in the former US Administration of the Antilles, and the subsequent dissolution of the Civil Administration, the island-nation of Martinique has inaugurated its independence with its first ever election. Now under the control of the reformist socialist Tertulien Robinel, the island has nominally separated from both the United States and France, though retaining considerable American ties.

International observers, initially predicting a win for opposition leader Victor Sablé and a smooth reintegration into the OFN, now note Robinel's moderate ideological approach and well-negotiated nationalisation of former American assets. Though opting not to fully join the OFN, the new government is touted by some as a demonstration of American state-building, remaining ideologically independent from the former administrator. More cynical publications note the strong influence of New Dealers and requests already made for financial aid.
strings.FWI_news.10.a: Only time will tell if this was a good choice.
strings.FWI_news.8.desc:
The overwhelming electoral victory of Aimé Césaire in the recent national elections for the island-nation of Martinique have resulted in the complete socialisation of the nation. Immediately after the swearing in of new deputies and officials, Césaire has proclaimed the formation of the 'People's Republic' of Martinique, backed by a new constitution officially affirming the country as a one-party socialist democratic republic.

International response has been muted, with unofficial sources from Washington suspecting electoral fraud and foreign interference from unnamed countries. Regardless of this, the new nation's outsized place as a Caribbean hub for Francophone leftism will undoubtedly send ripples throughout the region, and reports of labour organisation and student activism in nearby countries have already begun to sprout up.

strings.FWI_proxy.2.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

FROM FBI DIRECTOR J.EDGAR HOOVER
MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES

SUBJECT: UPCOMING REFERENDUM FOR AUTONOMY OF FORMER FRENCH WEST INDIES

1. Political activity in the islands has reached an all-time high in the months leading up to the vote, with notable spikes of protests in the population centers of Guadeloupe and Martinique. In spite of this, the local administrator, High Commissioner Lyman Lemnitzer, has reasonably managed to maintain order as of the time of writing.

2. Radical anti-US sentiment is rampant among the islanders, but not unanimous, leading to regular clashes between pro-independence and anti-independence groups. These advocates for continued American presence might prove to be a useful playcard in swaying public opinion for the impending ballot.

3. Our control over the civil administration allows us a high degree of freedom in the potential for covert action to steer the vote's result in our favor. Even in the case of an unfavorable outcome, the referendum's non-binding status means the situation generally remains of medium to low concern.

4. However, high levels of foreign influence is to be expected. Meddling from countries in the Mexican sphere of influence, and competing interests from European powers like Iberia might express a shift in the voter base, and should still be approached with caution.
strings.FWI_proxy.3.t: Report on the French Antilles Referendum
strings.FWI_proxy.3.desc:
DIRECCIÓN FEDERAL DE SEGURIDAD
ISSUE: U.S-organized referendum will decide the fate of the French Antilles.

Weeks of civil unrest have rocked Guadeloupe and Martinique, as the population expresses their grievances against the American occupation. The French Antilles have been under U.S “protection” since the Second World War, languishing in mediocre economic waters for years. It seems the recent tension has finally forced Washington's hand, and the population expects the upcoming referendum to bring decisive change.

There are two choices for the soon-to-be independent Antilles. The U.S favors a federation to keep Martinique and Guadeloupe united, retaining most of the structure of the existing American administration, ensuring their continued influence. Alternatively, the islands may vote to part ways as their own polities.

Mexico will put diplomatic and material support behind the democratic drive of the people of the Antilles, as they strive to achieve full independence. The anti-federationists represent the opposition to an American-orchestrated, artificial union. Backing them not only strengthens regional autonomy, but will provide Mexico with new economic and political associates, particularly in Martinique.

Very Respectfully,
Regional Director of Security
Colonel Emilio Torres.
strings.FWI_proxy.4.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL

TO THE AMBASSADOR TO THE UNITED STATES

FRENCH ANTILLES - MARTINIQUE AND GUADELOUPE, UNDER U.S OCCUPATION

A fresh opportunity to advance Iberian interests in the Caribbean presents itself with the incoming referendum on the status of the French Antilles. After recent civil unrest stemming from years of economic woe and frustration with the American occupation, the fate of the islands rests on the ballot box. Martinique and Guadeloupe will either become a federation beholden to American interests, or split into independent states.

The ambassador should notify the union government that limited resources should be put behind the anti-federationist campaign. The failure of Washington's federation scheme would break its hold over the islands' future and free them for Iberian investment. Adrift, the new power structures post-independence will also seek realignment. They'll find Iberia's arms wide open.

Supporting the anti-federationists in Martinique and Guadeloupe is the foremost priority for the Iberian government in the Caribbean.
strings.FWI_proxy.4.a: We want a drink from America's watering hole.
strings.FWI_proxy.5.desc:
Twelve hours after the referendum, the streets of Guadeloupe and Martinique were mostly quiet. The rising sun greeted the posters and flyers which have dominated the streets of Basse-Terre and of Fort-de-France, now left for the street sweepers and the annals of history. The people of the United States Antilles began filling the streets and going about their day as usual. The referendum came and went, not leaving much of a trace on the people's daily lives.

Twenty-four hours after the referendum, Commissioner Lyman Lemnitzer took to the airwaves, commending the people for fulfilling their democratic right and duty, and thanking them for believing in the future of the confederation. Lemnitzer reiterated that many of the institutions of the current Civil Administration will be retained, in order to speed up the transition to independence and a semi-presidential system.

Two days after the referendum, A group of three middle-aged men sitting in a cafe in Pointe-à-Pitre discussed their island's future. Two of them had voted for the confederation and the third against, but the debate was cordial enough. Things were looking up, the two supporters of the confederation said, and there was no point in rocking the boat. The third man wasn't convinced, but he couldn't convince them otherwise, either.

Five days after the referendum, a young man was hauled before the local court for having attempted to torch a police car in Le Lamentin. When questioned, he said he was acting in protest against the colonial authorities and of the confederation scheme, which, he claimed, “would only let the Americans press the boot on us more efficiently”. He was sentenced to two months in the local prison, joining his companions who had been imprisoned before the referendum took place.
strings.FWI_proxy.6.desc:
The headquarters of the United States Antilles Civil Administration was abuzz with frantic activity as the results of the recent referendum came in. In an unexpected setback to commissioner Lyman Lemnitzer's plans for the path of the islands towards independence, voters had rejected the Confederation scheme he had proposed. Now, the administration was put into a tailspin, having to rejigger its schedule and tie down the torn-up loose ends created by the result.

The first step in this process was currently taking place in Lemnitzer's office. The sleepless commissioner was receiving delegates from the island councils of Guadeloupe and Martinique, who had come to deliver almost identical resolutions - both islands would move to seek self-government as sovereign polities. Mustering his diplomatic skill, Lemnitzer smiled, shook hands, and then smiled once more for the cameras and proclaimed something about how “The United States of America remains a steadfast guarantor of democratic rights and the right to self-determination”. But he couldn't help but feel defeated.

With the failure of his plan, Lemnitzer knew his services would not be required here very soon. He had come to enjoy his job, but he was more worried about the ability of the islands to establish stable, cordial systems of government without America's - his - backing. The Caribbean was a geopolitical battleground, and small nations tended to get swept up in the storm.

As the representatives of the two islands left, Lemnitzer sat down, alone and exhausted. The two large files were now sitting on his desk, waiting for him to deliver them to D.C. He almost wanted to refuse. To keep the files here, maintain a strong hand, and help the people of these islands achieve their independence with the help of America's guiding hand. But he knew it couldn't be done. He had asked the people what they wanted, and they wanted him out. He wasn't in control anymore.
strings.FWI_proxy.6.a: And soon, Congress would ratify that fact.
strings.FWI_proxy.6.b: The Caribbean grows a little choppier. And that suits us just fine.
strings.FWI_proxy.6.c: Another blow dealt to imperialism. A small step for sovereignty in our hemisphere.
strings.FWI_proxy.8.t: Sing Me A Song, Oh Pianoman
strings.FWI_proxy.8.desc:
The horizon began to turn a vague shade of orange, tinged with the blue still pervading, and with his eyes turned towards it, Salvador Gallástegui left work. It was a slight liberty, of course, he was heading out early. But he had already fulfilled what Mexico had really wanted that day - a few statements welcoming Martiniquan and Guadelopean independence, a few photoshoots with nationalist politicians, a meeting discussing potential issues that might split them diplomatically. He could have ten minutes to himself.

Taking a moment, he strolled across the waterfront of the Canal Levessoir, looking out towards the waves. Distant, exuberant crowds talked among themselves, talking excitedly about the future. Those who had opposed it, of course, wouldn't be out. He took a brief look at the American embassy, lights still on but lacking movement at the front beyond one intern. Clearly, his efforts at supporting Antillean independence had paid off, and it was only his low ranking that stopped the contingency meeting from taking place.

There were a few hours where the result looked a little narrower, and where the United States mulled emphasizing that it was a nonbinding referendum. But as soon as rumor got around, the streets were packed with demonstrators disguising their fury under celebration, marching by his office, and they decided to climb down and accept the terms.

Sitting on a bench overlooking the Palais de Justice, he took out a guitar, and began to strum. It was an idle tune, a handful of chords connected only by the echoes of his notes. Nonetheless, people slowly began to gather, listening to the tune, couples clapping as he came to the end of one flourish and individuals humming to it as they slowed. As he took another look around, he began to take mental notes about the crowds and sorted their growing relief into the outline for a later report.
strings.FWI_proxy.8.a: Even a stubbed toe may fell a prizefighter.
strings.FWI_proxy.9.desc:
Fernando María Castiella's room echoed with laughter. First out of shock, and then out of relief, Castiella laughed at the report in front of him. Antillean voters had chosen to reject American plans to centralize, and had instead chosen independence. No images were provided, but the report provided details on how wide the celebrating crowds were, and how strong the result was. Across every island, a decisive majority had pushed for independence, and were only just beginning to retire for the evening.

Taking a moment to relax, he poured himself a wine, derived from a 1960 Portuguese vintage. It wasn't particularly old, but it was still a year to commend. He savoured the taste before moving to write some messages. The network of planters across Martinique and Guadeloupe he had contacted had definitely pulled through, and that deserved some reward. A few trade deals, some travel permits, some gifts. Enough to reward them for their work smuggling Iberian propaganda and goods into the Caribbean.

For a moment, he had feared all of his work would be lost. In the last days of the campaign, the Americans had begun to campaign - first through sympathetic media outlets and then through ambassadors - that it was a non-binding referendum, and he had lost all hope. But with how decisive this margin was? With how large the demonstrations were? He picked his old plans back up. If anything, he began daring to expand them. He just had to find his notes first, and-

The laughter was replaced by a swear. Of course! He'd lost his notes! Over the last few months, as the referendum looked likely, he had begun researching and developing plans for building political and economic ties to the Antilles! When the Americans had tried to downplay it, he threw them away! Scrambling to the phone, he called his secretary, demanding that she search through the rubbish. No matter how stained or crumpled, he needed those notes if he were to move ahead.
strings.FWI_proxy.10.desc:
The two officials sat in a nondescript restaurant on the outskirts of Washington, D.C., a growing pile of cigarettes filling the ashtray between them. Sometimes, the small, dark place allowed for more open conversation than halls of the State Department headquarters, with less prying eyes and more loud chatter.

One of the men stubbed another cigarette on the table. “This thing with the Antilles shouldn't have gone the way it did, man. It wouldn't have been too hard, either. Just annul the results and go forward with the more responsible plan. We've protected them from the fascists for two decades now, they should have known better. Maybe we could have let them have a little referendum to ratify everything when it's all said and done”.

His companion raised an eyebrow. “Really, John? We let them have this referendum, and the results were clear. You can't just erase 67 percent of the vote like that. Once we've gone ahead with the vote, we've committed ourselves to respecting the results. Even if they've let irresponsible demagogues get their way.”

John nodded bitterly. “Oh, get off that high horse, Bruce. The president wanted to annul the results too, until the FBI told him about a ”high chance of violence“ if he did. Suddenly he praises the results and promises a smooth transition to self-rule. Violence, my ass. The fascists are just going to jump at the opportunity the moment we're gone and build another Dominican Republic. All because we've been too cowardly to truly defend democracy.”

Bruce leaned back. “I don't know, man. I think you're overreacting a bit. They'll still be in the OFN, after all. And if they really slide towards fascism...
strings.FWI_proxy.11.desc:
Guadeloupe knew no seasons. Its soaring heat remained constant year-round, from which General Lyman Lemnitzer's little nocturnal ritual was the only relief, as he took his usual fresh night air bath on the hotel's balcony. He also didn't mind the view from this modest observatory, where he could gaze upon most of Basse-Terre's dormant streets.

His own little slice of the Caribbean, the unwanted prize for years of service overseeing America's finest defeats. It pained him to admit it, but he had started growing rather fond of the humble little fiefdom. It had never liked him back, of course; yet at times like this, where the quiet was undisturbed, he could almost convince himself otherwise.

Perhaps that was why he felt a hint of sadness knowing that as soon as morning came, these very streets would never be so peaceful again.

It was no surprise, really. Though a part of him had wished differently, his impromptu séjour to the Antilles wasn't going to be interrupted any time soon. In an unusual display of consideration, the heads in Washington had even given him advance notice of the President's decision to ignore the referendum's results and enforce a renewal of the Short-Fulbright Act. So now, until the statement's release at dawn, he had an entire sleepless night to ponder where it had all gone wrong.

Perhaps he was to blame for even submitting the proposal to Congress to begin with. For entertaining any hope that it wouldn't backfire as spectacularly as it did. No, maybe he was actually to blame for creating the situation that led to this in the first place. For mishandling the domain he was so generously granted by old Kefauver. He knew the locals definitely blamed him for all their troubles, the manifest representative of everything they hated about the American intruders. He sighed, taking one last look at the serene small town.
strings.FWI_proxy.11.a: Most of all, he knew he would take the fall for what was going to happen next.
